summary: Describes graceful restart for OSPFv3, which lets a router restart its routing software while neighbors keep forwarding traffic to it. It is identical to the OSPFv2 version except for differences such as the format of the grace LSAs. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When a worker takes a quick restart, coworkers keep the work going and do not panic. OSPFv3 graceful restart lets a router restart without everyone rerouting.

questions: what is the ospfv3 grace lsa type
why must ospfv3 interface ids be preserved on restart
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routers announce a graceful restart, using a grace-LSA of their own type.

tldr.problem: An OSPFv3 router whose forwarding plane is intact may need to restart its control software without neighbors tearing down its adjacencies and rerouting traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The router floods a grace-LSA (LS type 0x000b) carrying a grace period and a reason code, and neighbors keep advertising it as fully adjacent. The restarting router also keeps its LSA ID to prefix mapping and its Interface IDs unchanged.
tldr.outcome: It reuses the OSPFv2 graceful restart method of RFC 3623 with a different grace-LSA format and a few OSPFv3-specific rules.

today: RFC 5187 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3623.

sections.title: Graceful Restart for OSPFv3
sections.content: Graceful OSPF restart (RFC 3623) lets a router restart the control plane of OSPFv2 while its forwarding plane stays intact, with minimal disruption to the network. In general the same methods work for OSPFv3. This document covers the differences, chiefly that OSPFv3 uses a grace-LSA with a different format to signal that a router is starting, or is about to start, a graceful restart.
sections.eli5: The restart idea already existed for the older OSPF. This paper explains the few changes needed for the newer one.

sections.title: The Grace LSA
sections.content:
A router doing a graceful restart originates grace-LSAs. A grace-LSA asks the router's neighbors to help by continuing to advertise it as fully adjacent during the specified grace period. It carries the grace period and a reason code.

In OSPFv3 neighbors on any link are always identified by router ID, whereas OSPFv2 uses IPv4 interface addresses on broadcast, NBMA and point-to-multipoint links. For that reason the router-address TLV of RFC 3623 is not needed in OSPFv3. The TLV formats otherwise stay unchanged.
sections.eli5: Before leaving for a short break, the router hangs a note on the door saying how long it will be gone and why, so neighbors keep its seat.

sections.title: Grace-LSA Type and Format
sections.content: A grace-LSA has LS type 0x000b, function code 11. The S2 and S1 bits are 0, meaning link-local flooding scope, and the U-bit is 0 because it does not apply to link-local scope. The Link State ID is the Interface ID of the interface originating the LSA. After the standard LSA header come TLVs, formatted per Section 2.3.2 of RFC 3630, each with a Type, a Length and a Value.
sections.eli5: The note has a standard label on the outside, then the details inside as little labeled slots.

sections.title: Grace Period and Reason TLVs
sections.content:
Two TLVs can appear in a grace-LSA, and both MUST always be present.

  • Grace Period (Type 1, Length 4): the number of seconds neighbors should keep advertising the router as fully adjacent, regardless of database synchronization state.
  • Graceful restart reason (Type 2, Length 1): 0 unknown, 1 software restart, 2 software reload/upgrade, 3 switch to redundant control processor.
sections.eli5: The note says how many seconds the router will be away, and a number for why it is away.

sections.title: OSPFv3-Specific Rules for the Restarting Router
sections.content:
Two rules, both MUST, keep the restart from causing churn.

First, in OSPFv3 the LSA ID of inter-area prefix LSAs and external LSAs is just an unsigned 32-bit integer, not tied to the prefix as in OSPFv2. The restarting router MUST preserve the LSA ID to prefix correspondence across restarts.

Second, the Interface ID (Section 3.1.2 of RFC 2740) MUST be preserved. Link-LSA and Network-LSA IDs and link descriptions in Router-LSAs map to it, and a change would mismatch the router's old LSAs and neighbor state and end the graceful restart early. The RFC prefers putting this burden on the restarting router rather than synchronizing changes between neighbors. It notes many implementations use the interface's MIB-II IfIndex as Interface ID.
sections.eli5: When the router returns it must use the same labels and room numbers as before, or everyone gets confused and the pause ends early.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
OSPFv3 authentication (RFC 4552) relies on manual key distribution, so replay protection with sequence numbers is not possible. Replaying a grace-LSA could fool neighbors into thinking a router taken out of service is still restarting. The RFC says replaying ordinary Hello packets would achieve the same thing more easily, so the added risk is insignificant and no new security concerns arise.

For IANA, the value 0x000b was assigned in the OSPFv3 LSA Function Codes sub-registry. Grace-LSA TLVs use the existing OSPFv2 Grace LSA Top Level TLV sub-registry.
sections.eli5: Someone could copy the note to fake a restart, but faking a normal hello is just as easy, so this adds almost no new danger.
